title: Ivory Riot — London Art-School Editorial Spread
description: A Cavalry-magazine-styled collage built on five-plus rotated photo fragments and intersecting display type, anchored by a diagonal pull quote that rips across the optical center. The ink-arrow annotations and ivory paper ground give it the handmade urgency of a London art-school zine — distinct from digital-maximalism templates that rely on gradients rather than print texture.
philosophy: This template exists because some ideas are too loud for a clean grid and too urgent for comfortable white margins. It values collision over harmony, visual tension over visual rest, and the specific electricity of a composition that looks like it was built at 2am with scissors, a photocopier, and total conviction. It rejects corporate sterility, symmetrical stock-photo placement, and any layout that could honestly be described as 'balanced.' It is made for speakers whose authority comes from creative daring, not institutional calm.
goodFor: Portfolio presentations for creative agencies, art schools, or design studios
Brand-launch or campaign-reveal decks where raw visual energy signals confidence
3-line pull quotes that need to land viscerally rather than be read analytically
Cultural keynotes, festival openers, or awards nights with a design-literate audience
avoidFor: Chart-heavy quarterly business reviews requiring clear data hierarchy
Financial, legal, or compliance presentations where legibility is non-negotiable
Slide decks with more than three dense bullet points per view
Audiences with no prior exposure to editorial or zine design conventions
author: harness

examples.promptCore: The title slide feels like the cover of a zine assembled at two in the morning — urgent, tactile, and slightly threatening. Photo fragments compete for territory against oversized display type, the whole composition canted just enough to generate tension without tipping into chaos. Risograph ink grain and an ivory paper ground push every element into analogue materiality, resisting any reading of the slide as a polished digital artefact. Avoid smooth transitions, centred layouts, symmetric image placement, or any compositional choice that could honestly be called restful.

examples.layoutNotes: The title slide operates as a collision field rather than a grid: three to five photo fragments are pinned at conflicting rotations, with at least one bleeding past the slide edge and one cropped hard at the optical center. The deck title drives diagonally from the upper-left quadrant through the visual mass, layering over imagery and the bare ivory ground simultaneously. Subtitle and deck context land low-left in a deliberately off-balance anchor, countering the weight cluster above — no centering, no margin buffer, no symmetry axis. An ink-arrow or hand-scrawled annotation marks the subtitle zone as a structural accent, not a decorative afterthought.

examples.promptCore: The slide feels like a Cavalry editorial page torn out and pinned to a studio wall at midnight — urgent, handmade, completely convinced of itself. Photo fragments collide with oversized type rather than politely yielding to it, building a deliberately uncomfortable reading rhythm that demands attention before it allows comprehension. Ink annotations and rough-cut edges give the composition the texture of a physical artefact reproduced on a photocopier one generation too many. Avoid any zone of visual calm, symmetrical image placement, or type that sits safely within a gutter.

examples.layoutNotes: Fragmented base grid abandoned in favor of overlapping collision zones: two or three rotated photo fragments anchor the left bleed and lower-right corner while the primary content — a single declarative statement or short pull quote — slashes diagonally across the optical center, its baseline defying horizontal register. Ink-arrow annotations punctuate the negative space, pointing inward toward key words or cutting through a fragment edge. A section counter or folio mark sits lower-left as a hand-stamped artifact; no header band is used. Hierarchy is enforced by extreme scale contrast between the display statement and any supporting micro-copy, which tucks tight against a photo fragment rather than occupying its own safe column.
